key_finding: A nudge that shrouded the minimum-payment autopay option cut the fraction of cardholders paying exactly the minimum by 23% after six months, but did not significantly reduce credit card debt.
methodology: Field experiment on live credit card accounts, six-month follow-up, mechanism analysis via liquidity constraints.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's central question — enrolment/behaviour change from a nudge can move the nominal metric (minimum-only payers) without moving the outcome that matters (debt), which is the exact 'vanity enrolment' worry support raised about the round-up feature.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not a savings product
shrouding is a different mechanism than opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrolment
relevance_reason: Consumer, self-directed, liquid financial product showing a default-like nudge changes nominal behaviour without changing the underlying amount, which is the trade-off the brief asks about.

key_finding: Synthesises plan-design literature: automatic enrollment and default investment options raise short-term participation but can suppress longer-term participant engagement.
methodology: Narrative state-of-the-art overview of DC retirement plan design research; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a recent synthesis of the engagement-suppression concern behind the support team's objection, useful as background even though the setting is an employer plan.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer app product
overview, not a source of new effect sizes
relevance_reason: Recent review touching on the persistence/engagement trade-off the brief is deciding, but in the employer-plan setting the brief says does not carry over directly.

key_finding: Argues default enrollment raises short-term participation but induces behavioural inertia — low contribution rates, account churn, and passive non-management over time.
methodology: Narrative policy discussion, abstract-only, no primary data reported.
why_it_matters: Restates the 'passive trap' concern already better evidenced elsewhere; low novelty and no effect sizes limit how much it should move the design decision.
limitations: employer retirement setting
no citations to date, unclear rigor, no quantitative estimates in the abstract
relevance_reason: Thematically on-point (defaults as passive trap) but thin evidentiary content compared to stronger papers in the set.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for when default effects persist or decay downstream, driven by time course of choice, antecedent preferences, and salience of trade-offs.
methodology: Conceptual/theoretical synthesis and research agenda across the consumer default-effects literature; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a framework for predicting exactly the question the brief asks — whether the entry-default effect on the round-up feature will persist at 6–12 months or decay — and what moderators (salience, antecedent preference) to measure.
limitations: theoretical synthesis, not a new empirical estimate
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: General consumer-behaviour framework for downstream default persistence, directly usable to design what to measure post-launch.

key_finding: Default enrollment in Medicare Part D has large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization; beneficiary passivity is remarkably insensitive even to substantial losses from staying in a bad default, and active-choice variation is driven by transitory shocks rather than attentiveness.
methodology: Three natural experiments with random assignment to default options in a large administrative health-insurance dataset.
why_it_matters: Strong evidence that default persistence is not conditional on the default being 'good' — relevant caution for whether a pre-set multiplier will simply stick regardless of fit, and that active-choice behaviour may not reflect genuine preference.
limitations: government health-insurance program, not a consumer fintech product
low-income beneficiary population differs from the app's user base
relevance_reason: Rigorous natural-experiment evidence on default persistence and the (in)sensitivity of passivity, directly bearing on whether the round-up default would similarly entrench regardless of fit.

key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and of default contribution auto-escalation; steady-state saving rates rise by only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of employees escalate on the first date.
methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job separation, balance withdrawal, and opt-out from auto-escalation.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of the support team's objection: default-driven enrolment lift shrinks sharply once turnover, withdrawal, and later opt-out are accounted for — directly bears on whether opt-out enrolment for the round-up feature is a real gain or a vanity metric.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated setting differs from a self-directed app
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults durably raise saving, with real effect sizes, which is exactly the counter-evidence the brief asked the scan to surface.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment for low-income employees in Germany's public pension raised participation by 23 percentage points, though most affected individuals subsequently opted out; the effect is stronger when incentives are high and awareness of enrolment status is low.
methodology: Nationwide policy natural experiment linking administrative and survey data.
why_it_matters: Sizeable, well-identified default effect estimate, plus a moderator (lack of awareness) that is a live manipulation-risk concern for an opt-out design in the app.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension, not a consumer fintech product
no measure of amount saved or retention beyond initial opt-out decision
relevance_reason: Provides a large recent default-effect estimate and a mechanism (awareness) relevant to whether opt-out for the round-up feature would read as manipulative.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains at 12 months are substantially attenuated by 36 months, though it still reduces inequality in savings; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans plus a representative UK panel; structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete decay trajectory for a default's effect over time (12 vs 36 months), the exact horizon the brief cares about for evaluating persistence of the round-up default.
limitations: retirement savings context, not liquid short-horizon consumer savings
switching-cost estimate is model-derived, not directly observed
relevance_reason: Quantifies default-effect decay at the 36-month horizon the brief specifically asks about, even though the setting is retirement rather than consumer savings.

key_finding: Defaults on financial risk-taking have medium-to-large effects, but implementing a default nudge (especially one the client rejects) lowers ratings of the advisor's honesty and advice quality, and framing of the default question shifts outcomes.
methodology: Three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207) on default and framing effects in financial advice.
why_it_matters: Direct European consumer-financial evidence that a rejected default carries a reputational cost — exactly the dark-pattern risk the brief flags for EU consumer protection — and that how the default is framed changes uptake independent of its level.
limitations: wealth-management advice context rather than a savings-pot feature
risk-taking outcome, not enrolment/contribution amount
relevance_reason: European, consumer-financial, experimental evidence on when a default is perceived as manipulative — precisely the reputational-risk question the brief raises for opt-out design.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment drove participation above 85%, but roughly 80% of participants initially accepted both the default 2–3% savings rate and default conservative fund, with half still at the default rate and fund after three years.
methodology: Administrative data from three large firms analysing pre/post automatic-enrollment participation, contribution, and investment choices.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a pre-set default level anchors the contribution rate people end up at for years — the foundational result behind the brief's anchoring question, even though newer papers should be weighted more given the app's different context.
limitations: employer 401(k) plan, not a consumer app
undated/classic study predates the mobile, liquid, EU-regulatory context the brief says has since changed
relevance_reason: Foundational evidence for level-anchoring by defaults, the phenomenon the brief's pre-set-multiplier decision is testing against, even though it is the older pension literature the brief wants to weight less heavily.

key_finding: Default adherence in consumer tipping decisions arises from complementary deviation cost and opt-out cost frictions — 84% of adherence requires both frictions together, and removing either largely eliminates the effect.
methodology: Structural model estimated on 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions, validated against a stated-preference survey.
why_it_matters: Names the specific mechanism (ease of opting out vs. cost of deviating from the default) that a designer can dial when choosing opt-in/opt-out/active-choice for the round-up feature, giving a quantitative handle on how much of any default effect is inertia versus preference.
limitations: tipping decisions, not a financial savings product
no data on persistence, amount saved, or financial-app users
relevance_reason: The friction-decomposition mechanism (deviation cost vs. opt-out cost) is a directly transferable design lever for how easy the round-up feature's exit or active-choice screen should be made.

key_finding: Opt-in enrolment in a liquid, withdrawable short-term payroll savings account was activated by at most 0.7% of eligible employees, but among activators 96% still had a positive balance and 87% received a contribution at month 12.
methodology: Field study of opt-in short-term savings account introduction at five UK firms, 12-month account-level tracking.
why_it_matters: The closest available analogue to the round-up feature — a liquid, withdraw-anytime savings account — shows opt-in produces very low take-up but excellent retention among those who do enrol, sharpening the enrolment-vs-engagement trade-off the brief is deciding.
limitations: delivered via employer payroll, so the 'trusted intermediary' effect the brief says doesn't transfer may inflate the observed retention
no comparison to an opt-out or active-choice arm
relevance_reason: Structurally the nearest real-world analogue to the round-up pot (liquid, employee/consumer short-term savings), showing opt-in's low-uptake/high-retention pattern the brief needs evidence on.

key_finding: Characterises when opt-out minimization versus maximization is asymptotically optimal as a default design, generalizing prior restrictive results, verified via simulation.
methodology: Theoretical welfare-economics model of optimal default design with asymptotic characterization and numerical simulation checks.
why_it_matters: Offers a normative framework for reasoning about which default (opt-in vs opt-out) is welfare-optimal given designer/user value alignment, useful for justifying the chosen entry design against a manipulation critique.
limitations: purely theoretical with simulated verification, no empirical population studied
abstract gives no domain-specific numbers applicable to savings products
relevance_reason: General normative theory of optimal default design that can frame the entry-design decision's welfare trade-offs, though it names no concrete population or setting to compare against the brief's.

key_finding: Develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations that EU law uses to distinguish acceptable choice architecture from regulable dark patterns, including pre-selected defaults.
methodology: Doctrinal legal analysis mapping EU dark-pattern law onto a normative autonomy framework. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly addresses the brief's reputational-risk concern: it gives the specific line EU regulators draw between a helpful default and a manipulative one, which should shape how the pre-selected multiplier and opt-out exit are worded and disclosed.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not empirical evidence of user behaviour
no data on enrolment or engagement effects
relevance_reason: Provides the EU regulatory framework for judging whether the opt-out or preset-multiplier design would read as a dark pattern, which the brief flags as a live risk.

key_finding: At a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had not opted out after 12 months, versus roughly half staying at typical lower defaults, and low-income employees were disproportionately anchored to a suboptimal rate.
methodology: Administrative data from a single employer's retirement plan with a very high default, compared against a literature review of lower-default plans. Abstract-only for effect sizes.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether the level of a preset default anchors people to a possibly-suboptimal contribution level, which bears on whether to pre-select 1x/2x/5x round-up.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app the employer does not mediate
single-employer natural experiment
relevance_reason: Closest available quantitative evidence on how the specific level of a default anchors contribution behaviour and who it disadvantages.

key_finding: Abstract text was not retrievable; title indicates large-scale UK field experiments on automating short-term (not retirement) payroll savings.
methodology: abstract-only — abstract text was corrupted/unavailable.
why_it_matters: If the underlying paper covers short-term, liquid savings automation as the title suggests, it would be one of the few studies matching the brief's liquidity constraint rather than the pension literature; but nothing in the record confirms this.
limitations: abstract not usable — no data, effect sizes, or methodology visible
title suggests payroll (employer-mediated) rather than app-based enrolment
relevance_reason: Topically closest to the brief's short-term/liquid savings framing among the shortlisted records, but cannot be scored on substance due to missing abstract.

key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into real-time text alerts reduced unarranged overdraft charges by 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges by 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in annual market-wide savings, though consumers still captured less than half of achievable savings.
methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments at major UK banks measuring the causal effect of automatic (opt-out) enrolment into alerts.
why_it_matters: This is a genuine consumer-banking automatic-enrolment study (not an employer plan), giving a real effect size for opt-out design in exactly the kind of app-based financial product the brief is building, and shows defaults help but leave real value on the table.
limitations: overdraft alerts are an information nudge, not a savings-level decision
no measurement of persistence beyond the experiment window stated in the abstract
relevance_reason: Directly on-domain: bank-app automatic enrolment with quantified effect size, the closest analogue to the round-up entry decision.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment into UK pensions raised savings (£32-38/month) but was partially offset by increases in unsecured debt (£7/month) and mortgage balances (£118), over 41 months.
methodology: Randomized policy roll-out of automatic enrollment across ~160,000 small UK employers, tracked over 41 months.
why_it_matters: Complicates the 'defaults simply add savings' story used to justify opt-out enrolment — some of the new savings is offset elsewhere in the household balance sheet, a caution relevant to claiming enrolment success as a clean win.
limitations: employer pension plan, not a self-directed liquid consumer product
debt offset mechanism may not transfer to small round-up sums
relevance_reason: Shows a genuine unintended consequence of opt-out defaults on net household finances, supporting the brief's request for evidence in both directions.

key_finding: Adding a single extra enrollment step (an 'ordeal') to a health-insurance auto-enrollment policy cut enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Natural experiment studying the removal/reinstatement of an auto-enrollment step in a public health insurance program, with a selection-market model.
why_it_matters: Direct evidence that adding friction (an active-choice-like extra step) to enrolment does not fall evenly — it screens out the people the feature might help most, a distributional risk the brief explicitly wants surfaced before adding an active-choice step.
limitations: health insurance selection market, not a consumer savings product
the 'ordeal' studied is a hard extra step, not necessarily the same as a single active-choice screen
relevance_reason: Directly informs C5/C6: the closest empirical evidence that adding a choice step disproportionately excludes vulnerable users, relevant to the active-choice design option.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults raised campaign donations by over $43 million but also increased refund requests by nearly $3 million, with the largest impact on small, inexperienced donors who did not compensate by changing donation amounts.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across political campaign websites that added pre-checked recurring-donation boxes at different times.
why_it_matters: The closest real-world analogue to a preset recurring-financial-commitment default: it quantifies both the enrolment lift and the harm (regret/refunds) concentrated on inexperienced users, exactly the distributional trade-off the brief is asking about.
limitations: political donations, not a savings product
no data on outcomes beyond ~months around the election cycle
relevance_reason: Same choice-architecture mechanism (pre-selected recurring financial default) as the round-up entry/level decision, with effect size and heterogeneity by user experience.

key_finding: A default option raises the reservation utility for search due to a reference effect, and those who reject the default self-select into finding better options, both effects confirmed experimentally.
methodology: Lab experiments testing a reference-dependent search model with and without a default option.
why_it_matters: Offers a theoretical mechanism for why defaults might anchor choice quality, but is generic to search behaviour rather than financial contribution levels.
limitations: abstract lab experiment, not a financial product setting
does not address contribution levels or enrolment specifically
relevance_reason: Provides a general behavioural mechanism (reference effect from defaults) that is only loosely analogous to anchoring on a preset multiplier.

key_finding: EU DMA-mandated browser choice screens raised Firefox usage by 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with the effect still growing 15 months after rollout.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design exploiting the staggered rollout of mandatory choice screens on iOS and Android under the EU Digital Markets Act.
why_it_matters: The largest-scale, most recent evidence on forced active choice under EU regulation — directly tests whether an active-choice screen produces durable behaviour change, the core question behind the brief's third design option, at persistence horizons (15 months) the brief specifically asks about.
limitations: mobile browser default, not a financial product
measures which browser is used, not amount of a financial commitment
relevance_reason: Same regulatory mechanism (mandatory forced-choice screen) as the active-choice onboarding option, under the same EU regulatory regime the brief operates in, with long-horizon persistence data.

key_finding: Generalizable active-choice interface designs let 98% of participants (of 410) exercise a privacy opt-out without feeling disrupted, a 40-point improvement over baseline schemes, while slightly reducing opt-out utility.
methodology: Usability study with 410 participants comparing nine privacy opt-out interface schemes in a browser extension, in a legal context that prohibits default-on settings.
why_it_matters: Offers interface-design lessons for how to make a mandatory active-choice screen feel non-disruptive rather than punitive, relevant if the team ships active choice for round-up onboarding.
limitations: privacy consent context, not a financial product
measures disruption/comprehension, not financial enrolment or amount
relevance_reason: Provides transferable UI-design guidance for making an active-choice (no-default) interaction usable, relevant to the active-choice onboarding option under EU consumer law.

key_finding: Switching university exam sign-up to opt-out increased nominal sign-ups but had no effect on effortful task completion across many exams, and only helped exam passing for students who were already responsive to university communication.
methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up from opt-in to opt-out, comparing sign-up rates against downstream effortful outcomes (participation, passing) and testing heterogeneity by responsiveness.
why_it_matters: The clearest available demonstration that a default can move the enrolment number while leaving actual effortful engagement unchanged for the majority — precisely the support team's disengagement objection, with a heterogeneity finding (works for already-responsive people, not others) that speaks directly to who is helped versus who is not.
limitations: university exam sign-up, not a consumer financial product
no direct financial-amount analogue to 'money saved'
relevance_reason: Directly tests the brief's central worry — nominal enrolment versus effortful downstream behaviour — with a heterogeneity analysis of who benefits, even though the setting is academic rather than financial.

key_finding: Making target-date funds the default investment option shifted stock allocations along the fund's glidepath by age, but contribution rates changed little following the policy change.
methodology: Account-level panel data on millions of U.S. investors, 2006-2018, exploiting the Pension Protection Act's effect on default fund status.
why_it_matters: Shows a default can reshape the composition of a financial choice (allocation) even while leaving the participation/contribution rate largely unmoved — a caution that defaults may change outcomes other than the one being tracked.
limitations: 401(k) investment-allocation default, not a savings-enrolment or contribution-level default
employer-sponsored retirement plan
relevance_reason: Marginally relevant analogy for the idea that a default anchors one dimension of choice (fund allocation) without moving contribution levels, but far from the brief's actual product.

key_finding: In an RCT of 220 participants, all tested nudges — including default options — significantly reduced willingness to contribute to voluntary pension savings relative to a control group, contrary to prevailing international evidence, with the strongest backfire from positive-narrative and default-option nudges.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey (n=220) testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on pension contribution decisions in China.
why_it_matters: A direct, explicit counter-example to the 'defaults always help' premise the brief asks us to test, showing defaults can backfire and reduce contribution willingness, with heterogeneity by income, education, and gender that bears on who is helped versus hurt.
limitations: small survey-based sample (n=220), hypothetical choices rather than real product behaviour
Chinese voluntary pension context, culturally and institutionally distant from an EU consumer app
venue is a minor conference-proceedings journal, raising quality concerns
relevance_reason: The one paper in this batch that directly contradicts the default-effect premise the brief asks the scan to test, with distributional heterogeneity data.

key_finding: People generally approve of financial nudges (rated positive on all dimensions except reverse-coded manipulation), with strong preference for System 2 interventions and savings-framed messages, across a representative sample of 2,100 Australians.
methodology: Pre-registered survey experiment presenting 2,100 respondents with 36 hypothetical financial intervention scenarios varying transparency, framing, and System 1/2 targeting.
why_it_matters: Directly measures when a bank-deployed financial default reads as helpful versus manipulative, informing the EU dark-pattern reputational-risk question for an opt-out round-up design.
limitations: Hypothetical vignettes rather than actual enrollment or savings behavior
Australian sample, not EU regulatory context
No round-up-specific product tested
relevance_reason: Bears directly on C5 (perceived manipulation/approval of bank nudges), central to weighing an opt-out design's reputational risk.

key_finding: Offering CCT beneficiaries a bank-account delivery choice had no significant average effect on savings, but raised balances among individuals with nonpositive prior balances.
methodology: Randomized experiment offering conditional cash transfer beneficiaries a choice between cash and bank-account deposit, tracking downstream savings and trust outcomes.
why_it_matters: Shows the benefit of an account-based savings mechanism is concentrated among those with little prior savings, informing who a round-up default would actually help versus leave unaffected.
limitations: Developing-country conditional cash transfer population, not consumer banking app users
Studies payment-channel choice, not an enrollment default
No enrollment-rate outcome reported
relevance_reason: Distributional evidence (C5) on heterogeneous savings response by baseline savings status, though the mechanism differs from a round-up default.

key_finding: Abstract fragment indicates compared automatic-IRA-with-emergency-savings program variants did not differ in contribution amounts or in liquid-fund availability.
methodology: abstract-only — comparison of automatic IRA program variants that include an emergency (liquid) savings component.
why_it_matters: Touches the hybrid liquid-savings-plus-retirement design question, relevant to whether a linked liquid pot changes contribution or enrollment patterns.
limitations: Abstract fragment gives almost no methodological detail or effect sizes
Still an IRA/retirement-oriented product, not a standalone consumer round-up app
relevance_reason: Closest available study pairing automatic enrollment with a liquid emergency-savings feature, relevant to the round-up product's liquidity.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment dramatically raised participation, and a substantial fraction of automatically-enrolled employees stuck to both the default contribution rate and default fund allocation.
methodology: Before/after quasi-experimental analysis of 401(k) savings behavior at a single large U.S. corporation around an automatic-enrollment policy change.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a default anchors not just enrollment but the contribution level itself, directly bearing on whether to pre-select a round-up multiplier, though in an employer-plan setting.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement plan; the employer-as-trusted-intermediary mechanism does not carry over per the brief
Single-firm case study
No consumer app or liquid savings context
relevance_reason: Foundational evidence that defaults anchor the contribution-level choice (C3), the mechanism underlying the multiplier pre-selection decision.

key_finding: Title indicates a comparison of savings behaviors between automatic-enrollment and voluntary-enrollment defined-contribution plan participants; no abstract text is available to state results.
methodology: abstract-only — comparative study design unspecified.
why_it_matters: Potentially a recent direct comparison of auto- vs voluntary-enrollment savings behavior, but without any abstract content its design impact cannot be assessed.
limitations: No abstract provided; methodology and effect sizes unknown
Defined-contribution employer plan setting, not a consumer app
relevance_reason: Recent (2026) auto-vs-voluntary enrollment comparison flagged by title alone; included for completeness despite missing content.

key_finding: Limited institutional trust and minority/non-national status are both associated with lower regular pension contributions and higher likelihood of early withdrawal once an early-withdrawal option was introduced.
methodology: Analysis of three representative Estonian surveys (2020–2022) surrounding a pension reform introducing an early-withdrawal option.
why_it_matters: Speaks directly to the support team's concern that passively-enrolled or low-trust users disengage and withdraw funds, flagging institutional trust as a driver of early exit — relevant to who is helped versus hurt by an opt-out design.
limitations: Mandatory pension savings context, not a self-directed liquid consumer app
Correlational survey data, not a causal test of default effects
Estonian institutional/regulatory context differs from a general EU consumer app
relevance_reason: Directly addresses distributional risk (C5) and post-enrollment withdrawal/disengagement (C2), core to the support team's counter-argument about vanity enrollment.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent survey experiment across G7 countries, prompting reflection on a hypothetical default (automatic booster enrollment) reduced stated vaccination intentions and policy approval rather than increasing support.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment testing reflection prompts on a hypothetical default-enrollment policy.
why_it_matters: Contradicts the premise that defaults 'just work' once surfaced to users: making the default salient produced backlash, a live analogue for the EU dark-pattern risk if users notice they were auto-enrolled into round-ups.
limitations: Health/vaccination policy setting, not consumer finance — decision structure and stakes differ substantially
Hypothetical vignette, not observed behavior
No enrollment-rate or amount-saved outcome
relevance_reason: Contradicting role: the finding that reflecting on being defaulted-in triggers backlash carries directly to the question of when an opt-out reads as manipulative once users notice it.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment and employer-matching contributions were both associated with higher retirement plan participation among U.S. Millennials in the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study.
methodology: Cross-sectional regression analysis of FINRA 2018 survey data controlling for debt, income, risk tolerance, and assets.
why_it_matters: Reconfirms the standard default-participation association in an employer setting but adds little beyond stronger employer-plan studies and doesn't isolate the default effect from matching.
limitations: Employer-sponsored plan with matching contributions, unlike a fee-free consumer round-up feature
Cross-sectional, non-causal design
No persistence or amount-saved outcome
relevance_reason: Marginal confirmatory evidence on default-participation association, included for completeness rather than new decision-relevant insight.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic employer contributions raised total saving substantially, while tax subsidies requiring active choice generated only about 1 cent of extra saving per dollar of subsidy, because roughly 85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but moved by defaults.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data analysis of the Danish population's retirement and taxable savings accounts.
why_it_matters: The strongest available effect-size evidence that passive/default mechanisms move real saved amounts, not just nominal enrollment, and that benefits are concentrated in a specific 'passive saver' segment — directly informs whether the round-up default would be a vanity metric or a real savings increase.
limitations: Danish employer- and tax-mediated retirement accounts, not a self-directed consumer banking app
Long-run wealth accumulation outcome, not the weeks-to-months round-up engagement window
No active-choice condition tested
relevance_reason: Landmark, large-sample evidence on whether defaults change actual saved amounts versus nominal participation, and on distributional heterogeneity between active and passive savers (C1, C5).

key_finding: Active choice, and an 'enhanced active choice' variant that highlights the loss from the non-preferred option, motivated behavior change effectively as an alternative to automatic enrollment, tested in field experiments.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice, building on the Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian & Metrick active-choice design.
why_it_matters: The closest prior work on whether active choice captures most of the enrollment benefit of a default without imposing one, and it proposes a specific enhanced-active-choice framing directly transferable to the app's onboarding screen for decision 1.
limitations: Field experiments in medication adherence and general behavior-change contexts, not consumer financial products
No round-up savings, persistence, or withdrawal data
Small-scale field trials
relevance_reason: Explicit method transfer: the active-choice and enhanced-active-choice mechanisms tested here are the exact onboarding designs the brief is deciding between (C6), regardless of the non-financial application domain.

key_finding: Synthesizes household-finance evidence that choice architecture, product design, and defaults are among the tools firms and governments use to shape saving, borrowing, and asset-allocation behavior, alongside education, disclosure, and price-based interventions.
methodology: Narrative literature review (NBER chapter) covering empirical regularities and behavioral interventions across household finance topics.
why_it_matters: Provides the broad synthesis view of where defaults sit among the household-finance intervention toolkit, useful context for weighing a default against alternatives like disclosure or education, though it offers no fresh effect sizes for round-up savings specifically.
limitations: General overview not focused on consumer savings apps or round-up features
No quantitative effect sizes reported in the abstract
Breadth over depth on defaults specifically
relevance_reason: Serves as a review-level synthesis of choice-architecture interventions in household finance, satisfying the brief's request for at least one review, despite predating app-specific evidence.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment raised participation above 85% at three firms; about 80% of new enrollees initially accepted both the low default contribution rate and default fund, and half still did so after three years.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms comparing automatic vs. opt-in 401(k) enrollment.
why_it_matters: Gives the clearest quantified persistence-of-anchoring evidence (default settings still holding at three years) directly bearing on both C2 and C3, and a caution that default-driven participation gains can be offset by low default levels — a check against assuming defaults straightforwardly help.
limitations: Employer 401(k) retirement plans, not a liquid consumer savings app
No active-choice comparison arm
Persistence measured over years, not the weeks/months timeframe relevant to round-up disengagement
relevance_reason: The classic foundational study quantifying both default-driven enrollment (C1) and long-run anchoring on default settings (C2, C3), against which later default-effect claims are measured.

key_finding: Randomized default enrollment into a salary-linked savings account increased participation by 40 percentage points — equivalent to a 50% matching incentive — driven by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of decision-making, and it also increased subsequent active saving after the study ended.
methodology: Field experiment in Afghanistan randomly assigning employees to different default configurations of a salary-linked savings account, with mechanism-testing interventions.
why_it_matters: Offers rare mechanistic evidence for why defaults work and shows the effect persisted into post-study active saving, informing whether a round-up default will drive lasting engagement or just nominal signup.
limitations: Salary-linked account for employees in a low-income-country context, not a self-directed consumer banking app
No test of active choice or preset contribution-level anchoring
Persistence measured as post-study active decisions, not months-long retention within the same feature
relevance_reason: Provides mechanism and persistence evidence for the default effect (C1, C2) in a liquid, non-pension savings account, closest in kind to the round-up product among the shortlist.

key_finding: A randomized reminder nudge in a Brazilian financial app cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use seeing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Field RCT with a financial management platform in Brazil; reminders for upcoming credit card payments tracked against downstream checking-account fee outcomes.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the support team's concern: a behavioural nudge that looks like a clear average win can concentrate harm on the most vulnerable subgroup, which is exactly the distributional risk the enrolment-default decision needs to be checked against before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or contribution-level anchoring
Brazilian credit/overdraft context rather than EU round-up savings
no measure of enrolment persistence or withdrawal behaviour
relevance_reason: Strongest available consumer-financial RCT evidence that a well-intentioned nudge can help most users while harming a concentrated subgroup, bearing directly on C5's distributional and manipulation-risk question for the opt-out design choice.
